figures.alt: Black-and-white photograph of two locomotives nose to nose, surrounded by a large crowd of workers and officials at Promontory Summit, Utah
figures.caption: The golden spike ceremony at Promontory Summit, Utah, May 10, 1869

options.misconception: Background: conflicts continued after 1869, including Little Bighorn in 1876 and Wounded Knee in 1890; the railroad intensified them.
options.text: The end of all conflict between settlers and Native peoples
Fast, cheap travel and shipping between the two coasts

options.misconception: Background: Utah became a state in 1896, nearly thirty years after the golden spike.
options.text: The immediate admission of Utah as a state

options.misconception: Background: railroads helped Plains farming grow by carrying wheat and cattle to eastern markets.
options.text: The end of farming on the Great Plains

rationales.A: Background: the railroad did not end conflict. It brought more settlers and soldiers west, and fighting continued, from Little Bighorn in 1876 to Wounded Knee in 1890.
rationales.B: Two locomotives nose to nose mean one connected line: passengers and freight could now cross the whole continent by rail instead of by wagon, ship, or stagecoach.
rationales.C: Background: Utah did not become a state until 1896, nearly thirty years after this photograph was taken.
rationales.D: Background: the railroad did the opposite for farming. It carried Plains wheat and cattle to eastern markets, helping farm country grow.
rationales.general:
Picture the two locomotives touching noses: two separate lines have just become one road across the continent.
1. Ask what a connected railroad changes. People and freight can move coast to coast in days, not months.
2. Rule out the grand claims. Statehood, peace, and the end of farming are not what a railroad delivers.
3. Name the direct result. Fast, cheap travel and shipping between the coasts.
Remember: a railroad's first gift is always movement — people and goods, faster and cheaper than before.

source: original; stimulus viewed before writing — photograph by A. J. Russell, 1869, public domain.
stem: The photograph marks the completion of the first transcontinental railroad. What did that railroad most directly make possible?

stimulus.source_note: Photograph by A. J. Russell, 1869. Public domain. Wikimedia Commons: https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Golden_Spike_ceremony,_Promontory,_Utah,_May_10,_1869.jpg
stimulus.text: The photograph shows two locomotives nose to nose at Promontory Summit, Utah, on May 10, 1869, surrounded by a crowd of workers and officials celebrating the driving of the golden spike. The Central Pacific line from the west and the Union Pacific line from the east met here, joining the continent by rail.
